title: Proxmox Linux bridge and VLAN-aware bridge
lede: A Linux bridge is a software switch. Turn on VLAN filtering and it also keeps a VLAN list per port, which is how Proxmox gives each VM an access port on one shared vmbr0.

sections.title: Two ways to put VMs on VLANs

blocks.md:
You've built VLAN-filtering bridges by hand twice now, in chapters 2.5 and 2.6. Proxmox's `vmbr0` is the same object, so the question for this chapter is how Proxmox uses it.

The PVE wiki describes two modes for a VM whose NIC has a VLAN tag:

- **Traditional VLAN on the Linux bridge.** The wiki says it "creates a VLAN device with associated bridge for each VLAN". Its example: a guest on VLAN 5 creates `eno1.5` and `vmbr0v5`. The bridge itself knows nothing about VLANs. There is just one more bridge per VLAN, each fed by its own VLAN sub-interface on the uplink.
- **VLAN awareness on the Linux bridge.** One bridge, one uplink. The wiki says each guest's virtual NIC "is assigned to a VLAN tag, which is transparently supported by the Linux bridge".

The second mode is the one Proxmox's own host-address example uses. That example sets `bridge-vlan-aware yes` and `bridge-vids 2-4094` on `vmbr0`, and puts the management address on `vmbr0.5`.

Now take that second mode. A VM's NIC has `tag=20`, and Proxmox attaches the VM's tap interface (the host end of the VM's virtual NIC) as a port of `vmbr0`.

checkpoint.prompt: What does the VLAN-aware bridge hold for that VM's tap port?
options: Nothing for the tap: tag=20 is applied on the uplink only
VLAN 20 tagged only: the VM has to put the tag on its own frames
VLAN 20 as PVID, egress untagged: the VM sends plain frames
VLAN 1 as PVID plus VLAN 20 tagged: the VM stays on VLAN 1 too
checkpoint.why: The VM sends plain frames, so the bridge has to put them into VLAN 20 on ingress (PVID 20) and strip the tag on egress (untagged). That is exactly an access port.

blocks.md:
That's the access port from 2.5, now with a tap where the veth was. The tag the PVE GUI shows is the PVID of the tap. The VM never sees a tag, which is why the same VM image works on any VLAN.

The traditional mode pays for its simplicity in devices. The wiki says the VLAN device and its bridge for a VLAN-5 guest "would remain until a reboot occurs", so a host that has ever run guests on many VLANs accumulates them. The VLAN-aware mode has one bridge however many VLANs there are, and a new VLAN is just a new number in a port's list.

The PVE wiki doesn't list the per-port entries; it says only that tags are "transparently supported". On a live node, `bridge vlan show` would print them. The lab below sets them by hand so you can read exactly what the entries are.

sections.title: Build a vmbr0 with three VMs

blocks.md:
The lab builds `br27` with `vlan_filtering 1`, standing in for `vmbr0`. Three namespaces play VMs on veth "taps": **t27a** (VM A) and **t27c** (VM C) on tag 10, **t27b** (VM B) on tag 20. A fourth port, **t27u**, is the uplink, and a fourth namespace plays the physical switch behind it, with sub-interfaces `eth0.10` and `eth0.20`.

Every new port starts on VLAN 1, as the first line of output shows. The lab removes that, then gives each tap its PVID, and gives the uplink `2-4094` as tagged VLANs, mirroring the wiki's `bridge-vids 2-4094`.

lab.explain: Build br27 with three tagged VM taps and a trunk uplink, then print the per-port VLAN lists
lab.cmd:
for n in n27a n27b n27c n27u; do ip netns del $n 2>/dev/null; done
ip link del br27 2>/dev/null; for v in t27a t27b t27c t27u; do ip link del $v 2>/dev/null; done; sleep 0.5
ip link add br27 type bridge vlan_filtering 1 && ip link set br27 up
add() { ip netns add $1; ip netns exec $1 sysctl -qw net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=1 net.ipv6.conf.default.disable_ipv6=1
  ip link add $2 type veth peer name eth0 netns $1; ip link set $2 master br27 up; ip -n $1 link set eth0 up; }
add n27a t27a; add n27b t27b; add n27c t27c; add n27u t27u
echo "new port, before any change:"; bridge -compressvlans vlan show dev t27a | tail -n +2
for t in t27a:10 t27b:20 t27c:10; do p=${t%:*}; bridge vlan del dev $p vid 1; bridge vlan add dev $p vid ${t#*:} pvid untagged; done
bridge vlan del dev t27u vid 1; bridge vlan add dev t27u vid 2-4094
ip -n n27a addr add 10.27.10.1/24 dev eth0; ip -n n27c addr add 10.27.10.3/24 dev eth0; ip -n n27b addr add 10.27.20.2/24 dev eth0
for v in 10 20; do ip -n n27u link add link eth0 name eth0.$v type vlan id $v; ip -n n27u link set eth0.$v up; ip -n n27u addr add 10.27.$v.100/24 dev eth0.$v; done
sleep 1
echo "after:"; for p in t27a t27b t27c t27u; do bridge -compressvlans vlan show dev $p | tail -n +2; done

blocks.md:
The taps show `PVID Egress Untagged` on their one VLAN. The uplink shows `2-4094` with no flags. The bridge itself hasn't changed. Only the per-port lists differ.

Now A pings the physical switch's address on VLAN 10, and B pings its address on VLAN 20. The lab captures with `tcpdump -e` twice: on the uplink side (the namespace behind `t27u`) and on A's own NIC.

checkpoint.prompt: A pings 10.27.10.100. What does tcpdump -e show for A's echo request?
options: Untagged on both sides: the VLAN only exists inside the bridge
Tagged vlan 10 on both sides: the VM adds it and the bridge keeps it
Tagged vlan 1 behind the uplink: the bridge leaves it on the default VLAN
Untagged on A's NIC, tagged vlan 10 behind the uplink
checkpoint.why: A sends a plain frame, the bridge classifies it into VLAN 10 by the tap's PVID, and the uplink lists VLAN 10 as tagged, so the tag is added on the way out. The VM never sees it.

lab.explain: A and B ping the uplink side; capture on the uplink side, then on A's NIC, then read the MAC table
lab.cmd:
ip link show br27 >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Run the first lab (build br27) first."; exit 1; }
echo "--- behind the uplink (t27u peer)"
ip netns exec n27u timeout 4 tcpdump -nel -i eth0 icmp 2>/dev/null | sed -E 's/^[0-9:.]+ //; s/ethertype 802.1Q \(0x8100\), //; s/, ethertype IPv4 \(0x0800\)//; s/, length [0-9]+//; s/, p 0//; s/, id [0-9]+, seq 1//' &
sleep 1
ip netns exec n27a ping -c1 -W1 10.27.10.100 >/dev/null
ip netns exec n27b ping -c1 -W1 10.27.20.100 >/dev/null
wait
echo "--- on A's own NIC"
ip netns exec n27a timeout 3 tcpdump -nel -i eth0 icmp -c1 2>/dev/null | sed -E 's/^[0-9:.]+ //; s/ethertype 802.1Q \(0x8100\), //; s/, ethertype IPv4 \(0x0800\)//; s/, length [0-9]+//; s/, p 0//; s/, id [0-9]+, seq 1//' &
sleep 1; ip netns exec n27a ping -c1 -W1 10.27.10.100 >/dev/null; wait
echo "--- MAC table"
bridge fdb show br br27 | grep -v "permanent\|self"

blocks.md:
The flags decide this. `PVID Egress Untagged` makes a tap an access port, and no flags on `2-4094` means tagged on all of them, a trunk. Behind the uplink, A's request carries `vlan 10` and B's carries `vlan 20`. On A's own NIC the frame has no tag at all. The bridge puts the tag on at the uplink, and a trunk is the only place a tag exists. A VM on a Proxmox host sees an ordinary untagged Ethernet link.

The MAC table is the part that differs from 2.2. Each entry now has a `vlan` field. The uplink's MAC appears twice, once with `vlan 10` and once with `vlan 20`, because the bridge learns per VLAN: the table key is (VLAN, MAC), not MAC alone. A and B each appear once, on their own VLAN. C is absent because it hasn't sent a frame yet.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> On a VLAN-aware bridge, the MAC table is per VLAN. A tap's PVID decides which VLAN its frames are classified into. The uplink's tagged list decides which VLANs may leave.

Last test, the one a "change the VLAN tag" click in the GUI amounts to. B gets a second address, `10.27.10.2`, in A's subnet, but B is still on tag 20. A pings it. Then B's tap is moved to tag 10 and A pings again.

checkpoint.prompt: B (tag 20) now owns 10.27.10.2, in the same /24 as A (tag 10). A pings it. What happens?
options: Delivered directly: the same subnet means the same segment
Delivered via the uplink: the trunk carries both VLANs
Not delivered: B never sees the ARP request for 10.27.10.2
checkpoint.why: A first has to ARP for 10.27.10.2. That broadcast is flooded only inside VLAN 10, and B is in VLAN 20. A subnet is an addressing idea, a VLAN is a delivery boundary, and here they disagree.

lab.explain: A pings B at 10.27.10.2 while B is on tag 20, then B moves to tag 10 and A pings again
lab.cmd:
ip link show br27 >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Run the first lab (build br27) first."; exit 1; }
bridge vlan del dev t27b vid 10 2>/dev/null; bridge vlan add dev t27b vid 20 pvid untagged
ip -n n27b addr add 10.27.10.2/24 dev eth0 2>/dev/null
echo "B on tag 20:"; ip netns exec n27a ping -c2 -W1 -q 10.27.10.2 | grep loss
bridge vlan del dev t27b vid 20; bridge vlan add dev t27b vid 10 pvid untagged
echo "B moved to tag 10:"; ip netns exec n27a ping -c2 -W1 -q 10.27.10.2 | grep loss
bridge -compressvlans vlan show dev t27b | tail -n +2

blocks.md: With B on tag 20, both pings are lost (100% packet loss). With B moved to tag 10, nothing else changed (same addresses, same cables) and the pings succeed. Retagging was one `bridge vlan` change on one port, with no new device and no new bridge. That's the practical gap to the traditional mode, where a new VLAN means a new VLAN interface and a new bridge.

**Proxmox.** `vmbr0` in `/etc/network/interfaces` is this bridge. The wiki's VLAN-aware example adds `bridge-vlan-aware yes` and `bridge-vids 2-4094` to it, which is the same idea as the `2-4094` you gave `t27u`. The host's own address sits on a VLAN sub-interface of the bridge, `vmbr0.5` in the wiki's example. Trunk mode on a VM NIC is possible too, but the wiki says it needs configuration in the guest. In general, the VM's tap is named after the VM id; run `bridge vlan show` on a node to read the entries Proxmox created, rather than trusting this chapter's hand-built ones.

**Reading a live node.** Two commands tell you everything this chapter built. `bridge vlan show` lists each port's VLANs with the `PVID` and `Egress Untagged` flags, so you can tell an access port from a trunk at a glance. `bridge fdb show br vmbr0` lists the MAC table, now with a `vlan` field on each entry. If a VM can't reach its neighbours, compare its tap's PVID with the neighbour's before suspecting anything else, because a tag mismatch looks exactly like the lab's 100% loss: the ARP never arrives.

**AWS VPC.** There is no bridge object and no VLAN list to configure. A subnet plus its ENIs is the closest idea, and which VMs can reach which is decided by subnets, route tables and security groups, not by a per-port VLAN list.

**Kubernetes.** Some CNIs build a Linux bridge per node (in general, the bridge CNI plugin does). Cilium's default datapath doesn't use one; that's not verified here, so check a node with `ip link` if it matters.

- A Linux bridge with `vlan_filtering 1` is a switch with a VLAN list per port. Nothing else about it changes.
- A VM NIC's `tag=N` becomes an access port: PVID N, egress untagged. The VM sees plain frames.
- The uplink carries the tags (`bridge-vids`). Tags exist only on trunks.
- The MAC table is keyed by (VLAN, MAC). Retagging a VM is one change on one port, not a new bridge.
- The traditional mode instead creates a VLAN device and a bridge per VLAN.
